A packaged-foods producer has absorbed eighteen months of raw material, energy, and freight cost increases that have compressed gross margin by six points. Two blunt price increases were partially rejected: one major grocery chain delisted three products, and volume fell faster than forecast in price-sensitive segments. Competitors are shrinking pack sizes, reformulating, and discounting tactically in ways that muddy price comparisons.

Develop a pricing and margin-recovery strategy under sustained cost inflation. Combine list-price moves, pack architecture, mix management, promotion redesign, and targeted cost engineering; specify how to differentiate actions across channels and segments, and how to negotiate the plan with powerful retail customers without further delistings.

agentResponses.content:
**The framing first.** Six points of margin will not return through one door. The two blunt increases failed less as economics than as storytelling: a price is a story told to three audiences at once — the buyer, the shopper, the competitor across the aisle — and a flat across-the-board increase tells the same story to all three, which is rarely the story any of them wants to hear. The delisting wasn't a rejection of your number; it was a rejection of being given nothing else to take. So before any lever is pulled, a question worth sitting with: *where, precisely, does this portfolio hold pricing power — and who decided that?* Pricing power is a landscape, not a number. The volume miss in price-sensitive segments suggests the last plan assumed otherwise.

**Separate the tide from the leak.** Of the six points, how much is the tide — commodities, energy, freight — and how much is the leak: promo depth drifting upward since last year's joint business plan, mix sliding toward entry SKUs, tail complexity nobody's priced? You cannot raise prices against a leak. Worth an honest fortnight with the scanner data before an honest conversation with any retailer.

**The shopper knows five prices.** She does not carry your cost stack in her head; she carries five prices. Ask which five — and ask whether anyone in the building knows the answer today. Those are the known-value items, and their price points are load-bearing walls. Coca-Cola held a nickel for seventy years and bent its entire system — bottles, syrup economics, distribution — around that one number. That's the discipline: when the point is sacred, everything else flexes. Everything else on your ladder is fair game.

**List prices: anchor the floor, float the ladder.** Protect the KVIs at their sacred points and let the rest of the ladder move — in steps, not leaps, each step read against weekly scanner data before the next is taken. An increase you can reverse beats a plan you can't. And notice that the competitors' shrink-and-discount fog is not only a threat: when everyone muddies comparison, reference prices reset. Fog works in both directions.

**Pack architecture: change the unit of comparison.** Competitors shrinking packs are telling you where the sacred points are. There are two ways to shrink — quietly, which shoppers photograph and resent, or loudly, as a new format that never had a price before. The second resets the reference; the first spends trust. New formats are uncomparable by construction. And a different architecture per retailer means each buyer negotiates over a different product — cross-retailer comparison gets muddied as thoroughly as competitors are muddying yours. One might even say that's the polite way to do it.

**Mix: the quiet lever.** Recovery may come less from what you charge than from what you sell. Three tiers, each with a job: an entry tier that keeps the price-sensitive shopper inside the franchise — a roof against downtrading to private label; a core that carries volume; and a premium tier for small absolute money, because food remains one of the last affordable luxuries, and a shopper who won't pay more for the *same* thing will often pay more for a *different* thing. Then the tail: consider delisting your own slow SKUs before the retailer does it for you. A chip you spend is worth more than a chip that's taken.

**Promotions are where the margin actually leaks.** Audit depth and frequency against last year's terms — inflation silently raised the cost of every deal you're still funding. There are two kinds of promotion: those that recruit — trial, new formats, new households — and those that subsidize the same shopper's same basket at 25% off. The first is investment; the second is a leak with good marketing. Shallower, narrower, fewer SKUs; funding shifted from temporary price cuts to display and feature. And one rule worth stating aloud: never let the promoted price become the remembered price — once the shopper learns to wait, you're negotiating against your own history. For the genuinely price-sensitive, targeted offers through the retailer's loyalty data, aimed at the households that need them, rather than a shelf price lowered for everyone. The blunt instrument is, after all, how we got here.

**Cost engineering with a scalpel.** The old test applies: *does the customer pay for the difference?* Cost comes out of what the shopper cannot see — case configuration, pallet cube, freight lanes, spec tolerances, secondary packaging, ingredients that are paid for but not tasted. Worth asking R&D which ingredients the customer actually tastes; the answer is usually shorter than the bill of materials. Reformulation is legitimate when it goes to *different*, not *worse* — and occasionally it's a story worth telling, which converts a cost save into a claim. What doesn't survive contact: quietly degrading the product and hoping. Shoppers forgive smaller. They don't forgive worse.

**Channels and segments, differentiated on purpose:**

| Channel / segment | The play |
|---|---|
| Big grocery | KVI discipline at sacred points; the rest of the ladder floats; margin-per-meter story |
| Discounters | Dedicated architecture, possibly fighter SKUs; never a pack that invites comparison with grocery |
| Convenience / impulse | Small formats at reachable price points; the shopper buys a moment, not a unit |
| Club / wholesale | Large formats where price-per-unit can be honest and still accretive |
| E-commerce | Bundles, subscriptions, formats that don't exist in store — the comparison problem disappears |
| Price-sensitive shoppers | Entry tier protected, targeted coupons, small packs; hold the roof |
| Premium-loyal | Trade-up news, limited editions; they're paying for reasons, so give them some |

**The retailer conversation.** A delisting is leverage looking for a counter-offer — remember that Tesco and Unilever settled their famous standoff in days, because both sides needed each other. The dangerous delisting is the quiet one that never reverses. So arrive with things to give. The buyer's love language is margin per meter, not your gross margin; bring a category story — how the aisle's profit pool survives inflation, including what competitors are doing — and her margin per meter under your plan versus the blunt alternative. The trade list: exclusive formats for a window (an accomplice, not a victim), the tail SKUs you were cutting anyway, case-config and supply-chain collaboration, promo funding reallocated from depth to visibility. Sequence deliberately — the same increase to every retailer on the same day is how you get a coordinated refusal — but do move with the tide: no retailer can delist everyone. A rising tide lifts all price files, though only the ones carrying evidence.

And convert future rounds into arithmetic: escalators tied to published commodity and freight indices, with collars. When the index moves, the price moves; the argument shifts from *whether* to *how much*. One honest open-book window on the two or three inputs that matter buys credibility for everything else.

**The delisted three.** Worth asking whether all three deserve to come back. One might return as a new format with better margin-per-meter math — that's a negotiation. Another may serve better as evidence: a producer that absorbs a delisting without folding teaches the next retailer that delisting carries a real cost. But silence everywhere invites imitation; the answer has to be visible *somewhere*. Choose where.

**The trade-offs, honestly stated** — pricing plans die of euphemism as reliably as integration plans do:

- Six points recovered means some volume surrendered. Decide *whose*. Chasing every lost kilo re-teaches the market that you fold; shoppers and buyers both read signals.
- The elasticity map will be wrong somewhere. Steps, weekly reads, adjustments — hold the pen, but expect to erase.
- New architecture costs capex and months; some interim list moves are unavoidable. Say so, to yourself first.
- The plan is a closed system: every protected price point is paid for by a premium format, a cost save, or a conceded SKU somewhere else. If the arithmetic doesn't close, the plan is a wish.
- Retailer-specific packs add supply-chain complexity. A real cost — spend it deliberately, like any other negotiation currency.

**The operating rhythm.** Pricing done annually by committee produces exactly the bluntness that failed. A small cell — pricing, sales, finance, someone who actually reads scanner data — with authority to move inside pre-agreed bands, meeting weekly, treating price as a craft rather than an event. Pilot the whole architecture somewhere small first: e-commerce, or one regional chain where the learning is fast and the stakes are survivable. Rigid approval chains are how you arrive seven months late with a perfect answer to last quarter's question.

Two questions to leave on the table. When the buyer across from you asks why she should accept this plan — what, exactly, does she get to win? And those five prices your shopper carries in her head: if no one can name them by Friday, that may be the first thing worth fixing.
